articles.title: Alberta overhauls high school graduation rules, giving students more course choice from 2028
articles.dek: The province will cut core credit requirements and drop mandatory senior math and science, while making physical education and a wellness and financial literacy course required in every high school year.
body: The Alberta government announced on Friday, Nov. 13, that it is changing what students must take to graduate from high school, a shift that will affect every Calgary high school once it takes effect in 2028 [1][2].

Students will still need 100 credits to graduate, but optional courses will be able to make up as many as 53 of those credits, up from 44 under the current rules [1]. Core credit requirements fall from 56 to 47 for students who start high school in 2028 [2].

In Grades 11 and 12, students will need 10 credits in English language arts, social studies or a combination of the two, rather than 10 credits in each [1]. They will need five credits in math or science, rather than five in each [1]. The Canadian Press reported that students will need only one senior English or social studies course and that senior math and science courses will no longer be required [2].

English, social studies, math and science will remain mandatory in Grade 10 [1]. Physical education and wellness will expand across Grades 10 to 12, and a wellness and financial literacy course will be required in all three years of high school [1][2]. Students must also write at least one diploma exam, in English language arts, social studies, math or science [1].
The changes will roll out in stages: Grade 10 students in fall 2028, Grade 11 students in 2029 and Grade 12 students in 2030 [1].
Education and Childcare Minister Demetrios Nicolaides said the province is not lowering the bar. "More flexibility does not mean lower expectations," he said [2].

The Alberta Teachers' Association disagreed with the approach. Its president, Jason Schilling, said Grade 12 English language arts and social studies are essential and that education partners were not meaningfully consulted on the proposal [1]. Bradey Thompson, principal and co-founder of Fusion Collegiate, said the current rules have served many students well but that students take different paths after high school [1].
The announcement does not change requirements for students already in high school, since the first group affected is students entering Grade 10 in fall 2028 [1][2].
key_facts: Graduation still requires 100 credits
Optional courses can count for up to 53 credits, up from 44
Core credits fall from 56 to 47
Starts with Grade 10 students in fall 2028

articles.title: Ottawa announces about $17 million in tariff relief for 18 Calgary-area businesses
articles.dek: A federal minister also promoted a new tax deduction for business investment at an event in southeast Calgary on Friday.
body: Eighteen Calgary-area businesses will share more than $17 million in federal money meant to help them cope with the effects of U.S. tariffs, the Government of Canada announced on Friday, Nov. 13 [1][2].

Eleanor Olszewski, the federal Minister of Emergency Management and Community Resilience and the minister responsible for Prairies Economic Development Canada, made the announcement at a news conference in an industrial park in southeast Calgary [1][2]. The event was held at the Shepard Industrial Park plant of Tech Wood Building Components [2].

The money comes from the Regional Tariff Response Initiative, a $3.45-billion federal program [1]. Each business receives up to $1 million as a non-repayable contribution [1]. The federal release lists the businesses as working in construction, advanced manufacturing, agriculture and health sciences, and puts the Prairie total administered by the agency at $17.6 million [1].

Three recipients were described in Calgary Herald coverage. Big Rock Brewery is receiving $850,000 to modernize its manufacturing, increase production, expand co-packaging and develop new drinks and packaging formats [2]. Fitness equipment maker Bells of Steel is receiving $1 million to improve its warehouse and speed up automation, and Tech Wood Building Components is receiving $1 million to expand and modernize its plant and add automation [2]. Olszewski said the funding will support 190 jobs in Calgary [2].

The minister also promoted the Productivity Mega Deduction, which the federal release says lowers the marginal effective tax rate on new business investment from 13 per cent to 6.4 per cent [1]. The Herald reported that it widens the types of assets that qualify, from about 15 per cent of assets to more than 65 per cent, covering items such as software, computer equipment, vehicles, pipelines and research and development [2]. Olszewski said the change will generate about $2.2 billion a year in economic activity over the next decade [2].
The sources describe the deduction differently: the federal release ties it to Budget 2026, while the Herald story calls it part of the recently tabled 2027 budget [1][2].

"Alberta businesses have always found ways to get things done," Olszewski said in the release [1]. The tariff initiative is part of a $7.5-billion federal package for workers and businesses affected by U.S. tariffs [1].
key_facts: 18 Calgary-area businesses get up to $1 million each
Money from the $3.45-billion Regional Tariff Response Initiative
Funding expected to support 190 Calgary jobs
Investment tax rate cut from 13% to 6.4%, federal release says

articles.title: Province proposes 10-year royalty break to spur new oilsands projects
articles.dek: The voluntary Oil Sands Growth Program would charge new projects and expansions a royalty starting at two per cent, rising to six per cent by year nine.
body: The Alberta government on Friday, Nov. 13, proposed a voluntary 10-year royalty incentive for new oilsands developments and expansions, called the Oil Sands Growth Program [1]. Premier Danielle Smith and Energy and Minerals Minister Brian Jean announced it at a news conference with Finance Minister Jason Nixon and industry representatives [1].

Under the design Jean described, companies would apply for the program, and projects would need approval [1]. It would be open to new greenfield projects and to brownfield expansions that meet a production threshold of 5,000 barrels per day [1].

Approved projects would pay a royalty of two per cent in years one to five, three per cent in year six, four per cent in year seven, five per cent in year eight and six per cent in years nine and 10 [1]. If the regular oilsands royalty rate is lower during that time, the lower rate would apply, and projects would return to regular royalties after 10 years [1].
The province expects to launch the program in early 2027, subject to program and regulatory requirements, and wants companies to start construction before the end of 2029 [1].

Smith said the province is aiming for about eight million barrels of oil per day by 2035 [1]. She said resource revenues have recently brought in about $20 billion a year, just over a quarter of the provincial budget [1]. "Investors have choices about where they put that money," Smith said [1].

The remarks did not include modelling or an estimate of what the incentive would cost the province in royalties, according to EnergyNow's report [1]. Kendall Dilling, president of the Oil Sands Alliance, estimated that more than $100 billion in upstream investment would be needed to fill proposed pipeline additions and expansions [1].

Executives from Cenovus, Suncor, Canadian Natural Resources, ConocoPhillips Canada, Strathcona Resources and Imperial were acknowledged at the announcement, and the Explorers and Producers Association of Canada also spoke [1].
key_facts: Voluntary 10-year royalty incentive for new oilsands projects and expansions
Royalty of 2% in years 1-5, rising to 6% in years 9-10
Expected to launch in early 2027
No cost estimate was given at the announcement

articles.title: Proposed city budget's fine print: higher fees, a bigger workforce and a costlier 2029 election
articles.dek: Details in the City of Calgary's proposed 2027-2030 budget include what each point of tax increase is worth and what it would take to trim next year's hike.
body: Documents behind the City of Calgary's proposed 2027-2030 budget contain a range of smaller items that council will weigh alongside the headline property tax increase, according to a review by LiveWire Calgary published Nov. 12 [1].

Each $25.6 million in spending equals one per cent on a typical single-family property tax bill [1]. Cutting five percentage points from the proposed 2027 increase would therefore take about $128 million in cuts or other measures, such as drawing on the Fiscal Stability Reserve [1]. Assessed values for all property types fell in 2026, so the city proposes raising the mill rate [1].

The city's workforce would grow from 19,411 to 22,946 positions by 2030, about 18 per cent [1]. The plan includes a new 11-person cyber security unit costing about $2.2 million a year, and councillors' office budgets would rise by $1.4 million a year from 2027, roughly $100,000 per ward [1].

The Calgary Police Commission's budget, unchanged at $1.39 million for eight years, would rise to $3.19 million [1]. The $28 million revenue loss from photo radar is funded for 2028 to 2030 but not for 2027 [1].

For transit riders, extending the transfer window from 90 to 120 minutes would cost $2 million a year [1]. Calgary Transit Access, the specialized transit service, needs another $1.4 million a year because contractor rates rose 25 per cent while funding covers 19.5 per cent, and some trips may be turned away [1].

Some fees would rise. One-day park programs would go from $270 to $395 and one-hour programs from $108 to $130, and a wedding at Devonian Gardens would rise about 13 per cent in 2027 [1]. A further $200,000 one-time grant would keep Inglewood Pool open until the MNP expansion is finished in the second quarter of 2027; without it, the pool would close at the end of 2026 [1].

The City Clerk is asking for $23.9 million for the 2029 municipal election, including $22.2 million for the election itself [1]. The 2025 election cost about $16 million and the 2021 election $8.5 million [1].

A zero-based review of city spending is not fully funded and may not begin until 2031 [1]. Council's budget deliberations are still ahead, and all of these figures are proposals that council can change [1].
key_facts: Each $25.6M of spending equals 1% on a typical house's tax bill
City workforce would grow about 18% to 22,946 by 2030
Police Commission budget would rise from $1.39M to $3.19M
2029 election request: $23.9M, up from about $16M in 2025

articles.title: Feeder main crews move to round-the-clock work Sunday as water use stays under 500 million litres
articles.dek: Calgarians used 477 million litres on Thursday, and the City is also repairing a water main leak in Edgemont that may lower pressure in five northwest communities.
body: Calgary used 477 million litres of water on Thursday, Nov. 12, keeping the city below its 500-million-litre daily target while Stage 4 restrictions remain in place, the City and CTV News reported Friday [1][2].

The City says keeping use under that line matters while the new Bearspaw South Feeder Main is connected, because the city is mainly relying on one water treatment plant [1]. Global News reported earlier this week that the Bearspaw plant normally supplies about 20 per cent of daily needs and the Glenmore plant the other 80 per cent [3].

What has changed since Thursday's update is the pace of work. Starting the evening of Sunday, Nov. 15, crews will work 24 hours a day for about two weeks at 33 Avenue and 89 Street N.W., where they are cutting into the pipe to install a new valve [1]. At the Shaganappi Pump Station, new pipe sections are in place and welding has begun, and asphalt removal started Friday at 83 Street N.W. [1]. Repairs to a smaller pipe segment along Parkdale Boulevard, between the Shaganappi and Memorial pump stations, are on schedule, with welding under way at two sites [1].
Drivers face single-lane alternating traffic and pedestrian detours at 83 Street N.W. and 33 Avenue N.W., and westbound turns onto 33 Avenue N.W. from 83 Street N.W. are not allowed [1].

Separately, the City began repairing a water main leak in Edgemont on Friday, a job expected to take about seven to 10 days [1]. Customers in Edgemont, Hamptons, Citadel, Hawkwood and Arbour Lake may notice lower water pressure, but the City says the water remains safe to drink [1]. Westbound Edgemont Drive N.W. is closed at Edgemont Boulevard N.W. [1].

As of Global's Nov. 9 report, restrictions were expected to stay in place for at least another three and a half weeks, and water chief operating officer Michael Thompson said the new pipe was expected to be in use by mid-December [3]. The City's latest update did not give a new end date [1].
key_facts: 477 million litres used on Nov. 12, under the 500-million-litre target
24/7 work starts Nov. 15 at 33 Ave. and 89 St. N.W. for about two weeks
Edgemont water main repair expected to take 7 to 10 days
Lower pressure possible in Edgemont, Hamptons, Citadel, Hawkwood and Arbour Lake

articles.title: Calgary police suspend Crime Stoppers partnership during federal privacy investigation
articles.dek: The move reverses the service's position from late October, when it said it would keep accepting tips through the program after a data breach at the tip platform's vendor.
body: The Calgary Police Service is suspending its partnership with Crime Stoppers while the federal privacy commissioner investigates a data breach, CTV News reported on Thursday, Nov. 12 [1][2].

The breach happened earlier in 2026 [1]. According to Global News, the U.S.-based company Navigate360 manages the platform Crime Stoppers uses to receive tips, and the company said a third party accessed one of its systems and copied data between Nov. 21, 2025, and March 5, 2026 [3]. Names, addresses and other sensitive information may have been affected, though the company said it found no evidence the information had been used for fraud or identity theft [3]. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada is investigating the company's safeguards [3].

The suspension is a change for Calgary. In an Oct. 30 report, Global News said a Calgary police spokesperson had confirmed by email that the service was continuing to accept tips through Crime Stoppers, and that police were satisfied with added security measures after talking with Crime Stoppers Canada [3]. Several other police services in Canada had already suspended their use of the program by then [3].

The scale of the breach has been measured elsewhere. In Toronto, 176,859 tips submitted between January 2022 and November 2025 were affected, including 12,392 that may contain personal information, according to the chair of Toronto Crime Stoppers [3].

The reports read did not say when the Calgary suspension will end or what the police service is asking tipsters to do in the meantime [1][2]. In earlier coverage of other suspensions, Global News noted that people can still report information through regular police channels, which are not anonymous, and should call 911 in an emergency [3]. People worried about their personal information were advised to contact Crime Stoppers directly [3].
key_facts: Calgary police suspend Crime Stoppers partnership
Federal privacy commissioner is investigating a breach at the tip platform's vendor
Data was copied between Nov. 21, 2025 and March 5, 2026, the vendor said
No end date for the suspension has been given

articles.title: Grey Cup Sunday brings road closures around McMahon Stadium; mild, partly cloudy weekend forecast
articles.dek: University Drive N.W. will close and Crowchild Trail will narrow from about 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. Sunday as Montreal and Edmonton meet in the 113th Grey Cup.
body: Drivers in northwest Calgary should expect closures and detours on Sunday, Nov. 15, when the Montreal Alouettes and Edmonton Elks play the 113th Grey Cup at McMahon Stadium [1]. Kickoff is at 5 p.m. and stadium gates open at 3 p.m. [1].

According to the City of Calgary details reported by Daily Hive, restrictions will be in place from about 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. [1]. University Drive N.W. will be fully closed between 16 Avenue and 24 Avenue N.W., with access limited to identified taxis, rideshare vehicles and vehicles with Grey Cup accreditation; residents can reach their homes through checkpoints by showing proof of address [1].

Crowchild Trail N.W. will be reduced to two lanes in each direction between 16 Avenue and 24 Avenue, with the speed limit lowered to 50 km/h and no left turns into the stadium area [1]. 23 Avenue N.W. will be closed between Crowchild Trail and Banff Trail N.W., and about 200 metres of Banff Trail N.W. will close near the Banff Trail CTrain station [1]. 24 Street N.W. becomes one-way northbound with a pickup and drop-off lane, and the public post-game pickup area is on 24 Street across Crowchild Trail, reached by the pedestrian overpass [1]. Temporary parking restrictions may apply in nearby neighbourhoods [1].
The City is encouraging fans to take Calgary Transit; Banff Trail station on the Red Line serves the stadium [1].

The weather should cooperate. CTV News forecasts a partly cloudy weekend with highs of 12 C to 14 C [2]. Grey Cup week festivities began in earnest on Thursday, when Calgary Grey Cup Committee chair Steve Sommerfeld rode a horse into a hotel lobby to kick off an annual tradition as fans arrived from across the country [3].

The game is the sixth Grey Cup held at McMahon, a 66-year-old stadium on University of Calgary land [4]. No decision has been made on a replacement; the City is running an early-stage feasibility study on major sports and event facilities [4]. Steve Allan, chair of the McMahon Stadium Society, told The Canadian Press, "It's time for a new building" [4].
key_facts: Kickoff 5 p.m. Sunday, Nov. 15; gates open 3 p.m.
University Drive N.W. closed 16 to 24 Ave. N.W., about 11 a.m. to 11 p.m.
Crowchild Trail reduced to two lanes each way at 50 km/h
Forecast: partly cloudy, highs of 12 to 14 C
